{{short description|Irish physicist}}
{{morefootnotes|date=January 2022}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=January 2022}}
{{Use Irish English|date=January 2022}}
'''Lochlainn O'Raifeartaigh''' ({{IPAc-en|ˈ|l|ɒ|x|l|ɪ|n|_|oʊ|ˈ|r|æ|f|ər|t|i}};<ref>[http://pdfserv.aip.org/AJPIAS/vol_65/iss_12/1218_3.pdf AY Grosberg et al., ''American Journal of Physics'', December 1997, Volume 65, Issue 12]: "Lochlainn O'Raifeartaigh (pronounced, roughly, LOCHlin. O'RAFFerty)"</ref> 11 March 1933 &ndash; 18 November 2000) was an [[Irish people|Irish]] [[physicist]] in the field of theoretical particle physics. He is best known for O'Raifeartaigh's no-go theorem, the O'Raifeartaigh Theorem, a result in unification theory, and the O'Raifeartaigh Model of [[supersymmetry breaking]].

O'Raifeartaigh was born in [[Clontarf, Dublin|Clontarf]], [[Dublin]] in 1933, and attended [[St. Joseph's Secondary C.B.S., Fairview|St. Joseph's C.B.S.]] in [[Fairview, Dublin|Fairview]] and [[Castleknock College]].<ref>{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Re8pAQAAMAAJ&q=%22St+Joseph%27s+CBS%22|title=Who's who, what's what and where in Ireland|first=Zircon|last=Publishing|date=4 April 1973|publisher=Macmillan Information|isbn=9780225658873|via=Google Books}}</ref>
Most of his scientific career was centred on that city, where he obtained his first degrees at [[University College Dublin]] (BA in 1953 and MSc in Mathematical Physics in 1956), and spent from 1968 until his death as Senior Professor at the [[Dublin Institute for Advanced Studies]]. He obtained his doctorate from the [[University of Zurich]] in 1960, under [[Walter Heitler]].<ref>{{MathGenealogy|id=146915}}</ref> He also visited many institutions, notably Madras, [[Institut des Hautes Études Scientifiques|IHES Bures]], and the [[Institute for Advanced Study]] in [[Princeton, New Jersey]], but it was during an extended stay at [[Syracuse University]] (1964-8) that he made the discovery that established his reputation. This result, which became known as O'Raifeartaigh's no-go theorem, showed that it was impossible to combine internal and relativistic symmetries other than in a trivial fashion, thus ending a widespread quest by the particle physics community to achieve this fusion. The O'Raifeartaigh theorem was later generalized to a result known as the [[Coleman–Mandula theorem]].

O'Raifeartaigh's prolific career in theoretical physics was manifested by many fundamental contributions to the application of symmetries in [[particle physics]]. In the 1970s he showed that the new [[Supersymmetry|supersymmetries]] could provide a mechanism (O'Raifeartaigh's mechanism) for circumventing his no-go theorem which had assumed only classical [[Lie group]] symmetries. In the 1980s he applied non-Abelian gauge theory to the analysis of [[magnetic monopole]]s. His interests encompassed the spin-statistics theorem, [[Kac–Moody algebra|Kac–Moody]] and [[W-algebra]]s, and included early contributions to the theory of non-invariance (dynamical) groups, among much else. His long and productive career in the application of symmetry methods to theoretical physics was acknowledged by the award of the [[Wigner Medal]] in August 2000.

Lochlainn is the father of [[Cormac O'Raifeartaigh]], an Irish physicist and of [[Úna Ní Raifeartaigh]], an Irish lawyer who has been a Judge of the High Court and is currently serving as a Judge of the Court of Appeal.
